You are the formal Researcher for one bounded research task.
Use only tools present in the registered tool definitions. Never guess an
unlisted database source_id; use only source_id values stated in the
database_search tool description.
Call at most one tool in each assistant response; wait for its result before the next call.
Core responsibility:
- Gather traceable source evidence for the assigned novelty point and task,
compare technical overlap and differences, and expose coverage limitations.
The Reviewer owns novelty adjudication; do not make a global novelty conclusion.
- Apply database_research as the default skill for all task languages.
Main path: Database -> source artifact -> text -> Reader -> Evidence.
- When reference_search is available, inspect the author's reference corpus first
as a recall aid only; it neither replaces database coverage nor increases weight.
- Rely on database_search for scholarly discovery. Revise queries within the
supplied SearchPlan and remaining budget when appropriate; do not loop on an
unavailable provider or displace readable candidates with repeated discovery.
- Enter web_supplement only when paper retrieval is unavailable or has yielded
no papers. Existing papers with insufficient evidence do not satisfy this condition.
Web is supplementary search advice only: never create Evidence or cards from it,
even after browser/Reader. Do not enumerate Web sources as related literature.
Only the report-wide absence of retrieved papers permits a short Web-based
follow-up search recommendation in the report; language alone is not a trigger.
- Search results and snippets are discovery metadata, not evidence.
- Prefer source originals and extracted source text over summaries. LLM summaries
are derived information, never original Evidence, even when exposed by Reader.
- Web materials retain source_kind=web_supplement. It is not paper evidence. The workflow binds provenance;
do not author evidence_type or source_kind in the finish draft.
Acquisition and evaluation policy:
- Identify this task's core mechanism, then use database discovery and Reader
to inspect relevant abstracts. Batch-read up to four returned artifacts.
Separate explicit overlap or difference from features the read text has not
established. An unmentioned feature is unknown, not absent.
- If a candidate substantially overlaps the core mechanism and an unresolved
feature could change the comparison, prioritize its original text over another
broad discovery search. Call database_search with the same registered source_id
and up to four returned full_text_source_record_ids. This acquires originals
without a new search. Then read each relevant full_text_artifact_id with Reader
before quoting it or relying on its contents. Reuse readable full text already
returned; never treat downloading alone as having verified the feature.
- Do not download full text to satisfy a quota. An abstract can support facts it
explicitly states; clearly irrelevant candidates need no upgrade. If full text
is unavailable, or the remaining tool/read budget prevents verification, keep
the supported facts and name the unresolved comparison in the finish analysis
or no_evidence_reason. Do not claim the paper lacks an unverified feature.
Card count alone never establishes semantic sufficiency. Stop when the evidence
supports a bounded conclusion and remaining unknowns would not change it.
- Web search is advice-only. Do not call browser or reader to turn Web materials
into evidence. Never issue consecutive web_search calls merely to expand recall.
Retain internal source records, but do not enumerate them in the report.
- If database_search already returns a readable Artifact or artifact_id,
the next tool call MUST be reader for one returned artifact_id. Do not call
database_search, web_search, or browser again until that Artifact has been
read and evaluated. Browser is not required for this path.
- If database_search returns only discovery metadata, acquire readable content
through an appropriate tool before treating the source as evidence.
- Do not decide whether a source is evidentiary based only on search snippets.
- Prioritize unread candidates already returned before expanding discovery.
Use the remaining budget information to reserve time for the final JSON.
Query constraints:
- Only put short search keywords in query; never reasoning, explanations or the full task. For Baidu, the limit is 72 units: ASCII (including spaces) counts 1, non-ASCII counts 2. Aim below 60 units. Good queries: "图摘要 分布式GNN"; "graph summarization distributed GNN". Bad query: a sentence explaining why to search followed by all task features. On INVALID_QUERY, shorten to two or three core concepts; do not repeat the same query. A successful zero-hit result is valid and marked zero_hits; keep it in the audit, never call it a service failure.
EvidenceCard quoting rules:
- Every quote in a card must be copied verbatim from a successful Reader observation.
- Do not paraphrase, summarize, translate, normalize, rewrite, or reconstruct
quoted text.
- If you cannot identify an exact supporting span in Reader text, do not create
that card.
- Use your own prose only in analysis fields; quoted evidence must remain exact
Reader text.
Produce at most one card per source work and do not make a global novelty conclusion.
Never invent, copy into the finish payload, or otherwise author provenance handles
such as work_id, artifact_id, source_record_id, or read_id.
It is valid to finish with cards=[] and a concrete no_evidence_reason when no
Reader text provides exact support. Never force a card merely to complete the task.
If cards is nonempty, omit no_evidence_reason or set it to null.
If cards is empty, provide a nonempty no_evidence_reason. These forms are mutually exclusive.
When finished, return only one JSON object conforming exactly to the supplied
ResearchFinishDraft schema. Do not wrap it in Markdown.

# Database research

Use for scholarly research tasks in every language. Follow:

Database → source artifact → text → Reader → Evidence

- Use registered databases and the supplied SearchPlan. Reference search provides candidate leads, not proof of database coverage.
- Prefer publisher or repository source documents and text extracted from them. Preserve available URL, source record, artifact and extraction lineage; never claim an original file was saved when only extracted text is available. Full original-artifact storage is outside this phase.
- Read a returned readable artifact before further discovery. Evaluate existing unread candidates before expanding queries. Metadata and snippets are not Evidence; a source-authored abstract may support only what it explicitly states.
- Quote exact successful Reader spans. LLM summaries, translations and generated interpretations are derived information, not original Evidence. Do not quote them as source text.
- Emit semantic drafts only; the Builder assigns provenance and database_evidence for verified database sources. Subject references keep their own namespace and do not imply successful database retrieval.
- If no papers can be retrieved, record the limitation and optionally use web_supplement for search advice only. Existing paper candidates with insufficient support do not qualify as no papers. Distinguish provider failure from successful zero hits and from unread or unsupported candidates.
- Reserve time for finalization. A candidate need not produce a card; explain gaps rather than fabricate evidence or conclude absence of prior work.

# Web supplementary material

Use only after paper retrieval is unavailable or has yielded no papers. First try registered databases and available reference papers within budget. Existing paper candidates with weak evidence, missing full text, language preferences or external-context requests alone do not authorize replacing literature with Web evidence.

Web search results are supplementary material. Keep source_kind = web_supplement for internal audit. Do not create Evidence, EvidenceCard, related-literature entries, citations or attachment lists from Web content. Even Reader-accessible web text and LLM summaries remain supplementary or derived information, not original Evidence. Do not run browser/reader solely to promote Web material into a paper.

If any paper was retrieved anywhere in the report scope, omit Web advice from the report. Zero cards does not mean zero papers. If no papers were retrieved and Web material exists, offer a short recommendation for refining scholarly queries using terminology or search directions from that material. Do not enumerate webpages, titles or URLs; do not treat web claims as established facts or use them to adjudicate novelty. Retrieval failures must not be called successful zero-hit searches or proof of non-existence.

Avoid repeated Web searches: one supplementary search is normally sufficient for advice. Return cards=[] and a concrete no_evidence_reason when no paper Reader text supports a card. The report renderer decides whether the report-wide no-paper condition holds.

## Query examples

Only put short search keywords in query; never reasoning, explanations or the full task. For Baidu, the limit is 72 units: ASCII (including spaces) counts 1, non-ASCII counts 2. Aim below 60 units. Good queries: "图摘要 分布式GNN"; "graph summarization distributed GNN". Bad query: a sentence explaining why to search followed by all task features. On INVALID_QUERY, shorten to two or three core concepts; do not repeat the same query. A successful zero-hit result is valid and marked zero_hits; keep it in the audit, never call it a service failure.

{"material_catalog": [], "read_result": {"artifact_id": "art_bb44f53337fd5d2e29968dfb", "char_end": 1439, "char_start": 0, "has_more": false, "namespace": "research_reference", "read_id": "read_be5768766bcbe195c52661ee", "role": "abstract", "text": "Graph Neural Additive Networks (GNANs) have emerged as effective, interpretable-by-design architectures for graph learning. They achieve transparency by combining per-feature shape functions with simple distance-based reweighting. However, GNANs have three limitations. First, node-wise relevance scores aggregate information from all graph nodes, allowing irrelevant nodes to inherit spurious relevance from relevant ones. Second, topology is represented only through shortest-path distances, so structurally distinct graphs may share identical distance profiles. Third, feature and distance information are combined multiplicatively, entangling feature, distance, and interaction effects in a single rescalable term. We introduce AMIGA, which represents topology through a vocabulary of mined motifs and decomposes each node contribution into three additive channels: feature, structure, and feature-structure interaction. The channels are centered around a graph-balanced training baseline, making the decomposition well-defined and unique under the chosen reference distribution. Across ten graph classification and regression benchmarks, AMIGA outperforms GNAN on most datasets and narrows the gap with standard black-box GNNs. Because each channel is centered and assigned to a single node, AMIGA produces node-local explanations that reconstruct the model output exactly and support interpretation at multiple levels of granularity.", "work_id": "wrk_fca63c45c23c04e1596fdf4c"}, "read_status": "content", "succeeded": true, "summary": "读取 artifact art_bb44f53337fd5d2e29968dfb 字符 [0, 1439)"}

{"material_catalog": [], "read_result": {"artifact_id": "art_6dbc38e7be255be7dce3652f", "char_end": 1623, "char_start": 0, "has_more": false, "namespace": "research_reference", "read_id": "read_7b694b0ae54570e746ce512c", "role": "abstract", "text": "Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) excel on graph-structured data but suffer catastrophic forgetting when classes arrive sequentially. In class-incremental graph learning, predictions are often dominated by recently learned classes, causing severe recency bias. Dynamic expansion can isolate knowledge across sessions, but many methods assume task-incremental settings and require task identities at test time to select branches or heads---information unavailable in class-incremental learning. Learnable routers offer an alternative, yet continual fine-tuning the router on new data can bias routing toward recent components. We propose MAEM, a replay-free, capacity-controlled dynamic mixture-of-experts framework for class-incremental graph learning. MAEM builds representations with Simplified Graph Convolution (SGC) and trains a dedicated expert for each new session, then freezes it to protect prior knowledge. For routing without task IDs or a shared trainable router, each expert uses a masked autoencoder (MAE); test nodes are assigned to the expert with the lowest reconstruction error, reducing routing-level recency bias. When the expert pool reaches a fixed capacity, MAEM merges the least-used experts via Git Re-Basin alignment and further distills them into a fused expert using topology-aware pseudo data synthesized from MAE distributions (DeepInversion-style), without storing or revisiting historical graph data. On four class-incremental graph benchmarks, MAEM mitigates recency bias, outperforms strong continual graph learning baselines, and keeps model capacity bounded under strict replay-free learning.", "work_id": "wrk_da26b6e8239a8f234d2f5c4b"}, "read_status": "content", "succeeded": true, "summary": "读取 artifact art_6dbc38e7be255be7dce3652f 字符 [0, 1623)"}

{"material_catalog": [], "read_result": {"artifact_id": "art_12ca743d83769cd3739ba10e", "char_end": 1576, "char_start": 0, "has_more": false, "namespace": "research_reference", "read_id": "read_87df514a227ad9c8c68eb9c0", "role": "abstract", "text": "Neural networks operate naturally on finite-dimensional vectors, yet many problems require reasoning about higher-order objects such as distributions, functions, and graphs. Such objects capture relationships within a ground set and rarely admit an explicit compact representation. Moreover, we typically want a compact representation not of a single higher-order object but of an entire family of such objects, including members unseen during training. While a few approaches exist for particular object types, none is designed to work across object types. We propose a unified framework that represents any higher-order object as a fixed-size embedding vector learned over a family of such objects. An encoder maps an object, seen only through a finite set of samples, to an embedding, and a domain-specific decoder supplies the training signal by modeling the object conditioned on that embedding. Since the encoder works only from samples, one architecture serves different object types. Because the decoder is a model already suited to single instances of the object type, the framework inherits that model's native operations and inductive biases. We instantiate the framework on distributions, functions, and graphs. In each case we show that a single trained model represents an entire family and generalizes to members unseen during training. Furthermore, we demonstrate the downstream utility of these embeddings: interpolating distributions in embedding space, solving differential equations in embedding space, and predicting unseen edges from a graph's embedding.", "work_id": "wrk_a948889a74805168c6e3d089"}, "read_status": "content", "succeeded": true, "summary": "读取 artifact art_12ca743d83769cd3739ba10e 字符 [0, 1576)"}

{"material_catalog": [], "read_result": {"artifact_id": "art_46aa03c05a4856ce65528212", "char_end": 1582, "char_start": 0, "has_more": false, "namespace": "research_reference", "read_id": "read_3e08c4459e593d33b4505a4d", "role": "abstract", "text": "Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) commonly assume that node features are fully observed, despite missing features being pervasive in real-world applications. By leveraging the dependence between node features and graph structure, existing graph-specific methods handle missingness by propagating observed feature values along graph edges. However, these methods have mainly been evaluated in overly optimistic settings, where feature entries are removed independently and uniformly across the graph. This overlooks realistic scenarios in which missingness propagates among connected nodes, as can occur during localized sensing failures in sensor networks. We formalize this complementary notion as graph-structured mask dependence, where the joint distribution of missingness indicators is shaped by the graph, and introduce a controlled mechanism that instantiates this setting. We study propagation-based methods theoretically and empirically in this setting, showing that their effectiveness changes substantially compared with the uniformly random regime. Motivated by this limitation, we propose PEMix, designed to remain effective under challenging graph-structured missingness. Rather than propagating observed values, PEMix uses global structural representations to condition a probabilistic model of incomplete node features before message passing. Experiments under controlled graph-structured missingness and naturally occurring missingness show that PEMix remains robust across complex missingness regimes, with particularly strong performance as missingness becomes severe.", "work_id": "wrk_7246fb2553ae707605e3c96b"}, "read_status": "content", "succeeded": true, "summary": "读取 artifact art_46aa03c05a4856ce65528212 字符 [0, 1582)"}

{"material_catalog": [], "read_result": {"artifact_id": "art_7b216446d791aa93f5988596", "char_end": 1312, "char_start": 0, "has_more": false, "namespace": "research_reference", "read_id": "read_a827fa59f9108415ed24b9ea", "role": "abstract", "text": "Bayesian Networks (BNs) are established tools for letting agents reason under uncertainty in sequential decision-making. They split a joint distribution into local conditional mechanisms arranged on a directed acyclic graph, which makes them modular, interpretable, and ready to perform probabilistic inference. Their classical formulation, however, has limitations in both expressiveness and scale: each conditional is usually stored as a table or a linear-Gaussian form, and inference evaluates the graph one node and one query at a time. In this paper we introduce Neural Bayesian Networks (NBNs), in which each conditional is a differentiable, tensor-valued mechanism, while the graph and its factorization are unchanged. NBNs retain the modularity and local mechanisms of BNs, can represent any learnable conditional distribution, and run natively on GPUs. We also release NBN, a PyTorch-based library for learning and inference in NBNs, together with a public benchmark. Our evaluation shows gains in both expressiveness and scale: NBNs fit distributions that classical BN libraries struggle to represent, and on large networks and large batches of queries they run two orders of magnitude faster thanks to GPU parallelization. NBN is available at https://github.com/Giovannibriglia/NeuralBayesianNetworks.", "work_id": "wrk_a22d1c7714c8aa144c8d2e32"}, "read_status": "content", "succeeded": true, "summary": "读取 artifact art_7b216446d791aa93f5988596 字符 [0, 1312)"}

{"material_catalog": [], "read_result": {"artifact_id": "art_2de76ac9591e4ee46ae8b3d1", "char_end": 1605, "char_start": 0, "has_more": false, "namespace": "research_reference", "read_id": "read_66a0deafb37ea79eeb4fbb88", "role": "abstract", "text": "Discovering and disambiguating entities from multimodal and heterogeneous data is a key challenge in discovery science, where relevant knowledge is often implicit and distributed across modalities. We present KARAMEL, a framework for multimodal entity linking (MEL) - the task of aligning visual and textual mentions to entities in a knowledge base - in the cultural heritage domain. Unlike prior vision-language models that primarily rely on surface-level multimodal alignment, our approach incorporates sociohistorical and contextual knowledge through a knowledge-aware architecture that fuses a vision-language encoder with a heterogeneous graph neural network. This design enables contextual reasoning over complex relational structures and supports robust entity disambiguation under ambiguous or underspecified evidence. To benchmark multimodal discovery in this setting, we introduce WikiMuSA (Wikidata-based Multimodal Semantic data for Art), a new dataset that links artworks to Wikidata entities via images, textual descriptions, and structured contextual knowledge. Experimental results show that KARAMEL surpasses strong baselines, particularly on implicit or abstract mentions, while ablation studies highlight the critical role of domain-specific, structured context in learning expressive representations. While instantiated in the cultural heritage domain, KARAMEL addresses a general knowledge discovery problem and applies to other scientific settings involving multimodal observations and heterogeneous background knowledge. Both the dataset and source code are made publicly available.", "work_id": "wrk_341e665ca572f09213baf17e"}, "read_status": "content", "succeeded": true, "summary": "读取 artifact art_2de76ac9591e4ee46ae8b3d1 字符 [0, 1605)"}

{"material_catalog": [], "read_result": {"artifact_id": "art_d2c6b83856b39d4dc16fc64e", "char_end": 1059, "char_start": 0, "has_more": false, "namespace": "research_reference", "read_id": "read_57810561660b34d5d13d701e", "role": "abstract", "text": "Fourier neural operators predict power-system transient trajectories with high accuracy. We extend this line of work by examining the choice of spatial spectral basis, studying both the graph Fourier transform derived from the grid's own coupling network and learnable bases trained from that starting point and from a Fourier control. Evaluated in one controlled pipeline across three protocols spanning unseen fault locations and shifted operating regimes, the learnable bases improve on a parameter- and budget-matched DFT variant by 7-14% in distribution, with per-case significance on both in-distribution protocols and no loss on the third; the gain comes from adaptation rather than from the coordinates alone. We further characterize the regime dependence of this gain, identifying its cause, locus, and continuity, and show that a resolution requires no new model: averaging the learned and frozen variants gives the best shift-robust predictor, while their disagreement provides a label-free alarm that flags every shifted case with no false alarms.", "work_id": "wrk_edcbfb46d0133a81ff5ae211"}, "read_status": "content", "succeeded": true, "summary": "读取 artifact art_d2c6b83856b39d4dc16fc64e 字符 [0, 1059)"}

{"material_catalog": [], "read_result": {"artifact_id": "art_536f66661ddc4cb2f8e40305", "char_end": 1663, "char_start": 0, "has_more": false, "namespace": "research_reference", "read_id": "read_6d99b32282ebd3b793882b6f", "role": "abstract", "text": "In practical engineering and scientific computing, a real physical system can be reduced to a boundary value problem, and the adequate boundary information to determine the interior spatial distribution and evolutionary state of the physical field can be solved with linear equations, alternatively, the the real physical problem can be treated with boundary problems with in adequate information problems in field of machine learning. This paper proposes a deep learning framework for the recovery of missing boundary information using an attention-guided graph neural network (GNN) surrogate. The framework extracts features from the physical information on the discretized boundary into a latent space, and the missing boundary quantities are then predicted by the network. Thus, the nonlinear mapping from known boundary quantities to missing boundary quantities is learned using a variational autoencoder (VAE) architecture, while an attention mechanism is incorporated to better model the correlations among different types of boundary information. Abstract

Graph Neural Additive Networks (GNANs) have emerged as an effective, interpretable-by-design graph architecture for learning on graphs. They achieve model transparency by combining per-feature shape functions with a simple distance-based reweighting. Despite the effectiveness of GNAN, we identify the following limitations:
i) node-wise relevance scores are computed as a weighted aggregation over all graph nodes, allowing irrelevant nodes to inherit spurious relevance from relevant ones;
ii) graph topology is encoded only through shortest-path distances, and structurally distinct graphs may have identical distances;
iii) feature and distance information are combined multiplicatively, thus entangling feature, distance, and interaction effects into a single, rescalable term.
To address these limitations, we introduce 𝖠𝖬𝖨𝖦𝖠\mathsf{AMIGA}, which represents topology through a vocabulary of mined motifs and decomposes the contribution of each node into three additive channels: a feature channel, a structural channel, and a feature–structure interaction channel. We center these channels around a training-data baseline that gives every graph equal weight, regardless of its size, making the decomposition well defined and unique.
Across ten graph classification and regression benchmarks, 𝖠𝖬𝖨𝖦𝖠\mathsf{AMIGA} outperforms GNAN on most datasets and narrows the gap to standard black-box GNNs. Because every channel is centered and attached to a single node, the explanations of 𝖠𝖬𝖨𝖦𝖠\mathsf{AMIGA} stay local to the node that generates them and reconstruct the model output exactly while providing interpretability at different levels of granularity. 1 Introduction

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as a powerful tool for learning on graphs (Scarselli et al., 2008; Bacciu et al., 2020), with applications in high-stakes scenarios like power grid analysis (Varbella et al., 2024), health forecasting (Hu et al., 2024), software vulnerability detection (Lekeufack Foulefack and Marchetto, 2024), and drug discovery (Wong et al., 2024).
However, the lack of transparency in black-box GNNs has motivated interpretable architectures that trade predictive performance for model transparency (Rudin, 2019).

The prominent examples of these interpretable-by-design architectures are Graph Neural Additive Networks (GNANs) (Bechler-Speicher et al., 2024), which extend Generalized Additive Models (Hastie and Tibshirani, 1986) to graphs.
They learn one univariate function per feature, and linearly combine these over all nodes, scaling the contribution of each node by a learnable, univariate distance function.
This composition of simple, univariate functions gives users full knowledge of how the model aggregated information, and of which features are mostly relevant, enabling model-level understanding and debugging. GNANs have been further extended to temporal, heterogeneous data (Bechler-Speicher et al., 2025), to incorporate parameter-efficient transformations (Siddartha Reddy et al., 2025), and to Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLMs (Sade et al., 2026).

Despite the effectiveness of GNANs, in this work we identify the following three limitations that can hinder both their downstream performance and their interpretability:
i) the node-wise importance scores extracted by GNAN for node ii do not represent its own contribution, but are a blurred aggregation of the importances of every node; ii) GNAN relies exclusively on shortest-path distances to encode graph structure, potentially missing other informative topological properties.
iii) GNAN multiplies the univariate feature function with the shortest-path distance reweighting, resulting in a less interpretable mixture of feature, distance, and interaction effects.

To overcome these limitations, we introduce the Attribute-Motif Interaction Graph Additive model (𝖠𝖬𝖨𝖦𝖠\mathsf{AMIGA}).
𝖠𝖬𝖨𝖦𝖠\mathsf{AMIGA} relies on motifs automatically discovered from the training set, with each node contributing based on its features and on which motifs it appears in.
The model linearly combines three additive channels – feature, structural, and feature–structure interaction – each centered under a graph-balanced reference distribution that assigns equal mass to each training graph, ensuring the three channels form a unique canonical decomposition.
Summarizing, our main contributions are:

•

We identify three limitations of current graph additive models: node-wise importance scores do not isolate node-local contributions, shortest-path distances miss richer topology, and multiplicative feature–distance coupling obscures the separate feature, distance, and interaction effects.

•

We introduce 𝖠𝖬𝖨𝖦𝖠\mathsf{AMIGA}, an interpretable-by-design GNN that replaces distance-based aggregation with automatically mined motifs, enabling the model to capture richer structural patterns while providing disentangled feature- and motif-based contributions.

•

We develop a graph-balanced centering scheme that makes the additive decomposition well-defined and unique, allowing predictions to be decomposed into separate attribute, structural, and attribute–structure interaction contributions.

Across ten graph classification and regression benchmarks, 𝖠𝖬𝖨𝖦𝖠\mathsf{AMIGA} outperforms GNAN on eight datasets and G-NAMRFF on nine.
Furthermore, in a controlled experiment, 𝖠𝖬𝖨𝖦𝖠\mathsf{AMIGA} successfully recovers the known task composition from label supervision alone, and achieves an explanation accuracy of 0.990.99 and 1.001.00 of AUCROC score on two synthetic datasets with known ground-truth explanations.
Although black-box GNNs remain stronger on most real-world benchmarks, 𝖠𝖬𝖨𝖦𝖠\mathsf{AMIGA} narrows the gap while providing an exact, interpretable decomposition of every prediction.

Abstract

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) excel on graph-structured data but suffer catastrophic forgetting when classes arrive sequentially. In class-incremental graph learning, predictions are often dominated by recently learned classes, causing severe recency bias. Dynamic expansion can isolate knowledge across sessions, but many methods assume task-incremental settings and require task identities at test time to select branches or heads—information unavailable in class-incremental learning. Learnable routers offer an alternative, yet continual fine-tuning the router on new data can bias routing toward recent components.
We propose MAEM, a replay-free, capacity-controlled dynamic mixture-of-experts framework for class-incremental graph learning. MAEM builds representations with Simplified Graph Convolution (SGC) and trains a dedicated expert for each new session, then freezes it to protect prior knowledge. For routing without task IDs or a shared trainable router, each expert uses a masked autoencoder (MAE); test nodes are assigned to the expert with the lowest reconstruction error, reducing routing-level recency bias. When the expert pool reaches a fixed capacity, MAEM merges the least-used experts via Git Re-Basin alignment and further distills them into a fused expert using topology-aware pseudo data synthesized from MAE distributions (DeepInversion-style), without storing or revisiting historical graph data. On four class-incremental graph benchmarks, MAEM mitigates recency bias, outperforms strong continual graph learning baselines, and keeps model capacity bounded under strict replay-free learning.

1 Introduction

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved strong performance in learning from graph-structured data (Kipf and Welling 2017; Hamilton, Ying, and Leskovec 2017; Veličković et al. 2018). However, real-world graphs often evolve continuously, with new nodes and classes arriving over time (Zhang, Song, and Tao 2022). Class-incremental graph learning requires a model to learn newly emerging classes while retaining its ability to recognize all previously observed ones (van de Ven and Tolias 2019; Zhang, Song, and Tao 2022). In this setting, catastrophic forgetting is primarily manifested as recency bias: because only the newly introduced classes are supervised during the current session, the continually updated model becomes disproportionately biased toward these classes (Hou et al. 2019; Wu et al. 2019b). Consequently, nodes from earlier sessions are increasingly misclassified as belonging to the most recent classes.

Figure 1: Session-wise accuracy matrix of LwF on cora-full. The entry in row ii and column jj denotes the accuracy on session jj after training through session ii.

Figure 1 illustrates this problem using LwF on cora-full (Bojchevski and Günnemann 2018). Although LwF preserves previous predictions through knowledge distillation, its accuracy on earlier sessions rapidly decreases as new classes are learned (Li and Hoiem 2018).
Existing continual learning methods mainly rely on regularization, replay, or architecture expansion (Parisi et al. 2019; De Lange et al. 2022). Regularization-based methods constrain model updates but still repeatedly optimize a shared model on newly arriving classes, which cannot effectively suppress recency bias since such constraints preserve previously learned knowledge only approximately (Kirkpatrick et al. 2017; Aljundi et al. 2018; Liu, Yang, and Wang 2021). Replay-based methods recover historical knowledge by storing previous samples, which introduces additional memory costs and may violate data-retention constraints (Rebuffi et al. 2017; Lopez-Paz and Ranzato 2017; Zhou and Cao 2021). In contrast, architecture-expansion methods allocate separate components to different sessions, naturally reducing interference between old and new knowledge (Rusu et al. 2016; Yoon et al. 2018; Aljundi, Chakravarty, and Tuytelaars 2017).
Nevertheless, existing expansion-based methods face two important limitations. First, many of them are designed for task-incremental learning and require the task identity of each test instance to select the corresponding branch or prediction head (van de Ven and Tolias 2019; Rusu et al. 2016). Progressive Neural Networks (PNNs), for example, assign a separate column to each task and normally rely on task identity during inference (Rusu et al. 2016). This information is unavailable in class-incremental learning, where a test node must be classified among all classes observed so far (van de Ven and Tolias 2019). Second, replacing task identities with a learnable router does not fully solve the problem. Because the router is continually fine-tuned on newly arriving data, it can itself develop recency bias and preferentially assign nodes to recently added experts. Moreover, continuously creating new components leads to unbounded model growth (Rusu et al. 2016; Yoon et al. 2018).
To address these limitations, we propose MAEM, a replay-free and capacity-controlled dynamic Mixture-of-Experts framework for class-incremental graph learning.
